question: How can superposed neural representations be reconciled with identifiable, human-interpretable latent features, and what would constitute quantitative evidence that sparse codes recover those features?

key_findings.claim: The paper proposes a three-link synthesis rather than a new recovery algorithm: representations can be identifiable up to linear transforms, superposition can compress more features than dimensions, and sparsity can select a more interpretable basis.
key_findings.evidence: The authors connect identifiability theory, compressed sensing and sparse coding to argue that apparent distributed representations need not preclude recoverable latent variables. The argument depends on structural assumptions and does not establish that every learned feature is a ground-truth factor.

key_findings.claim: Existing empirical evidence supports sparse decompositions as more human-legible than raw neurons, but interpretability remains evaluator- and metric-dependent.
key_findings.evidence: The survey reviews sparse dictionaries and sparse autoencoders whose features receive more coherent human or automated descriptions, while emphasizing that feature visualization, labeling and causal relevance measure different things.

key_findings.claim: Linear identifiability is not sufficient for semantic recovery.
key_findings.evidence: Latent representations can be determined only up to a family of transformations unless stronger assumptions are imposed; choosing a sparse basis adds an inductive bias but does not uniquely certify that the basis matches the world's causal variables.

key_findings.claim: Vanilla sparse autoencoders are one possible operationalization, not a theoretically optimal sparse-recovery method.
key_findings.evidence: The discussion contrasts reconstruction-plus-sparsity objectives with gated and thresholded variants and notes tension between reconstruction fidelity, feature splitting, dead latents and sparsity.

method.core_idea: Unify identifiability theory and the superposition hypothesis through sparse latent-variable recovery, then demand quantitative and causal tests of the recovered basis.
method.mechanism: Treat a network representation as a transformed latent code, impose sparsity to choose among equivalent bases, reconstruct activations with a learned overcomplete dictionary, and evaluate whether its features are coherent and behaviorally relevant.
assumptions: Task-relevant latent factors are sufficiently sparse or structured in the observed representation.
The representation preserves those factors through a recoverable transformation.
A sparse basis is closer to semantic factors than other equivalent bases.
Interpretability judgments and automated labels reliably track useful semantics.

techniques.role: Separates recoverability up to transformations from semantic uniqueness.
Uses an overcomplete sparse basis to decompose superposed activations.
Calls for explicit metrics beyond compelling feature examples.

evaluations.setting: Perspective review spanning representation identifiability, superposition and sparse coding.
evaluations.metric: Logical compatibility of theoretical results and reported empirical findings.
evaluations.result: The paper supplies a coherent conceptual bridge and research agenda, not a new benchmarked model or controlled experiment.
evaluations.baseline: Previously separate literatures on disentanglement/identifiability, toy superposition and sparse dictionaries.

evaluations.setting: Prior sparse-feature studies summarized by the authors.
evaluations.metric: Human or automated feature coherence, reconstruction and sparsity.
evaluations.result: Sparse features are often easier to describe than individual neurons, with known reconstruction and feature-quality tradeoffs.
evaluations.baseline: Raw neurons, PCA-like bases and dense activation dictionaries; evidence is heterogeneous across studies.

limitations: This is principally a synthesis/perspective and offers no new end-to-end empirical validation.
Identifiability results require assumptions that may fail in trained networks and usually leave transformation ambiguities.
Sparsity does not by itself imply causal, stable or human-meaningful features.
Feature interpretability metrics can reward fluent labels, cherry-picked examples or reconstruction artifacts.
The account does not resolve feature splitting, absorption, dead latents or cross-model alignment.
failure_modes: Dense or context-dependent factors cannot be recovered by a static sparse dictionary.
An autoencoder attains low reconstruction loss using arbitrary fragments rather than stable semantic units.
Automated explanations sound coherent while the feature has little causal effect on behavior.
A feature basis changes across seeds, layers or distributions, defeating claims of identifiable semantics.
reusable_insights: Keep mathematical identifiability, empirical recoverability and human interpretability as three separate validation targets.
Compare sparse-feature methods at matched reconstruction error and latent budget.
Test interventions on recovered features, not only top-activating examples.
Stability across seeds, models and distributions is a stronger semantic signal than a single compelling label.
open_questions: Which assumptions make sparse features identifiable beyond arbitrary linear transformations in real networks?
Can causal interventions distinguish genuine latent variables from reconstruction conveniences?
How should feature splitting and absorption enter an interpretability score?
Do feature dictionaries align across model sizes strongly enough to support scaling claims?

competitive_landscape.title: Toy Models of Superposition
competitive_landscape.difference: Toy Models provides constructive neural examples and geometric predictions for superposition; the reviewed paper connects that phenomenon to general identifiability and sparse-code recovery.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This predecessor trains and evaluates sparse autoencoders on language-model activations; the reviewed work is a broader theoretical synthesis and critique of what such evidence establishes.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: This work supplies large-scale empirical scaling laws and evaluation practice for SAEs, while the reviewed perspective focuses on conceptual conditions connecting sparsity to identifiable latent structure.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
competitive_landscape.difference: Scaling Monosemanticity demonstrates an industrial-scale feature dictionary and interventions; it remains empirical evidence subject to the semantic-identifiability caveats articulated by the reviewed paper.

novelty_assessment: The value is the unusually clear synthesis of three literatures and its insistence that interpretability become quantitative. It should not be read as empirical proof that sparse autoencoders recover unique ground-truth concepts: later scale demonstrations strengthen practicality, not the missing identifiability guarantees.
reviewer_notes: Read all 26 pages, including mathematical assumptions, compressed-sensing discussion, SAE variants, interpretability metrics and references. Four primary arXiv competitors were checked on 2026-08-23.
